questions.question: In our body, brain and spinal cord together constitute the:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**central nervous system**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The central nervous system (CNS) is comprised of the brain and spinal cord.
 
• The CNS is responsible for processing and transmitting information throughout the body.
 
• The brain controls most of the functions of the body including thought, memory, emotion, and sensory processing.
 
• The spinal cord acts as a conduit for signals between the brain and the rest of the body.
 
• The CNS is protected by the skull and vertebral column, as well as by cerebrospinal fluid.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Endocrine System**

 
 
• This system is responsible for hormone production and regulation.
 
• It includes glands such as the pituitary, thyroid, and adrenal glands.
 
 
 
• **Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)**
 
 
• This system consists of all the nerves that lie outside the central nervous system.
 
• It connects the CNS to the limbs and organs, essentially serving as a communication relay.
 
 
 
• **Autonomic Nervous System (ANS)**
 
 
• This is a part of the peripheral nervous system that controls involuntary bodily functions.
 
• The ANS regulates functions such as heart rate, digestion, respiratory rate, and pupillary response.

questions.question: The plant part moves toward light, it is called _________.
questions.solution:
Option **1** is correct:

__
 
• **Phototropism **is the ability of a plant or other **photosynthesizing organism**, to grow directionally in response to a light source.
 
• Plant and other autotrophs need to manufacture their own food; they usually do this through** photosynthesis**.
 
• Through photosynthesis, organisms convert **water**, **carbon dioxide (CO₂) **and light into **sugar**, which is used for energy and growth.
 
• Plants can not move around to acquire what they need, so in order to maximize the amount of light that they receive through the leaves, they use **phototropism**.
 
• **Positive phototropism**__ is the response of a plant toward a light source, while **negative phototropism** causes growth in the opposite direction.
 
• If the plant parts i.e.** stem** moves towards the light, show **positive tropism**. And if the plant part that is** root** moves away from light, then it shows **negative tropism**.

questions.solution:

• **Calcitonin**

 
 
• It is a thyroid hormone that controls the balance of calcium in the body. 
 
• The thyroid gland is the largest endocrine gland in the human body.
 
• Thyroxine and Calcitonin are the hormones secreted by the **Thyroid gland.**
 
• Calcitonin lowers the concentration of calcium in blood whenever it rises above the normal value.
 
• The normal level of calcium in the blood is **8-10 mg/dL.**
 
 
 
• **Insulin**
 
 
• **​**It is a protein hormone produced by beta cells of the pancreatic islets.
 
• It is considered to be the main anabolic hormone of the body.
 
• It regulates the metabolism of carbohydrates, fats and protein by promoting the absorption of glucose from the blood into the liver, fat and skeletal muscle cells.
 
• The absorbed glucose is converted into either glycogen via glycogenesis or fats via lipogenesis.
 
• Beta cells are sensitive to blood sugar levels so they secrete insulin into the blood in response to a high level of glucose.
 
• Insulin helps to keep the blood sugar level from getting too high (hyperglycemia) or too low (hypoglycemia).
 
 
 
• **Testosterone**
 
 
• **​**Testosterone is the only male sex hormone present in the human body, which causes physical changes in puberty, increases bone density and muscle mass, growth of facial, pubic, and body hair, deepening of the voice, and is also responsible for sexual and reproductive development.
 
• Testosterone is the main sex hormone in men, which is naturally produced in the testes and in small amounts by the adrenal glands.
 
• Testosterone belongs to a class of male hormones called androgens, which are also known as steroids.
 
 
 
• **Estrogen**
 
 
• **​**​This group of hormones is responsible for developing female sexual characteristics.
 
• **Secreted from the ovaries.**
 
• Estrogen is also produced by the placenta during pregnancy to help maintain a healthy pregnancy.

questions.solution:
When a plant shows growth movement in response to a stimulus, it is referred to as tropism. Depending upon the direction of the stimulus, plants can show either positive or negative tropism.

**__Positive Tropism__: **When the movement is towards the direction of stimuli, it is referred to as positive tropism.

**__Negative Tropism__: **When the movement it is away from the stimuli, it is termed as negative tropism.

Tropism Types include:

**__Geotropism__: **

__
 
• It is a type of tropism where plants show growth in response to gravity.
 
• Stems/Shoots of a plant show upward movement, which is termed as negative geotropism.
 
• Roots shows positive geotropism by growing downwards.

 

This can be explained with the help of the following diagram:

In general, the stems usually show positive phototropism, while roots show negative phototropism.

**__Chemotropism__: **When plants grow in response to certain chemicals, this type of response is known as chemotropism.

**__Hydrotropism__: **The movement or the growth of a plant in relation to the stimulus of water is called hydrotropic movements and the equivalent response to the stimulus of water is called hydrotropism.

questions.question: Select the INCORRECT statement related to tropism.

options.text: Geotropism - in response to the pull of earth or gravity

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Phototropism - movement towards water**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Phototropism** is the growth movement of a plant in response to light. Plants typically grow towards the light source, which is known as positive phototropism.
 
• It is primarily regulated by the plant hormone auxin, which redistributes towards the shaded side of the plant, causing cell elongation and bending towards the light.
 
• Phototropism helps plants maximize light absorption for photosynthesis, which is essential for their growth and energy production.
 
• Unlike hydrotropism, which involves movement towards water, phototropism involves movement towards a light source. Therefore, the statement "Phototropism - movement towards water" is incorrect.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hydrotropism**

 
 
• Hydrotropism is the growth response of plant roots towards water. This allows the plant to maximize water uptake, which is crucial for various physiological processes.
 
• Unlike phototropism, which is influenced by light, hydrotropism is influenced by moisture gradients in the soil.
 
 
 
• **Geotropism**
 
 
• Geotropism, also known as gravitropism, is the growth response of plants to gravity. Roots typically exhibit positive geotropism (growing downwards), while stems show negative geotropism (growing upwards).
 
• This response ensures that roots anchor the plant and access water and nutrients, while stems grow towards the light.
 
 
 
• **Thigmotropism**
 
 
• Thigmotropism is the directional growth response of plants to touch or physical contact. It is commonly observed in climbing plants and vines.
 
• Examples include tendrils of pea plants wrapping around a support structure.
 
 
 
• **Chemotropism**
 
 
• Chemotropism is the growth response of a plant to a chemical stimulus. For example, the growth of pollen tubes towards ovules during fertilization is driven by chemotropic signals.
 
• This type of tropism ensures that fertilization occurs successfully within flowering plants.

questions.question: Human growth hormone is secreted by which gland?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Anterior lobe of pituitary gland.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

 
• The** anterior pituitary** is the **front lobe** of your pituitary gland, a **small, pea-sized organ found **beneath your hypothalamus at the base of your brain.
 
• Your** pituitary gland** is an **endocrine gland** that regulates the operation of several other endocrine glands.
 
• The **anterior (front) lobe and posterior (back) lobe **make up your pituitary gland.
 
• The anterior pituitary gland produces and releases a total of **six hormones** that govern a variety of cellular functions, including: growth, metabolic rate, reproduction, the body's reaction to stress or trauma and lactation.
 
• Your **pituitary gland** has a** total diameter** of roughly **1/3 of an inch,** or about the size of a pea.
 
• The **anterior pituitary is larger** than the posterior pituitary and makes up roughly** 80% **of your pituitary gland's overall weight.
 
• **Six major hormones **produced and released (secreted) by the anterior pituitary:
 
 
• **Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH, or corticotropin)** is a hormone produced by the** adrenal glands.** Your adrenal glands (the glands on top of your kidneys) are stimulated to **generate cortisol** and other hormones by this hormone.
 
• **Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)** is a hormone that stimulates the **production of sperm i**n the testes and **eggs and oestrogen** in the ovaries.
 
• **Luteinizing hormone (LH) **encourages women to ovulate and men to produce testosterone.
 
• **Growth hormone (GH) **is a hormone that **promotes growth **in children. Growth hormone aids in the maintenance of** healthy muscles and bones** in adults, as well as influencing fat distribution.
 
• **Prolactin** is a hormone that increases the **production of breast milk **after a baby is born and can impact menstrual cycles, fertility.
 
• **Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)** causes your thyroid to create hormones that control your **metabolism, energy, and nervous system.**

questions.question: Which of the following is the basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Neuron**__.

 
• **The neuron** is also known as **neurones or nerve cells**.

 
 
• The **fundamental unit of the brain and nervous system are neurons**.
 
• The **basic structural and functional unit **of the nervous system is called the neuron.
 
• There are **three** major types of neurons:
 
 
• **Sensory neurons**
 
• **Motor neurons**
 
• **Interneurons**.
 
 
 
 
 
• **The nephron** is the** structural and functional unit of the Kidney**.
 
 
• It is made up of a **renal corpuscle and a renal tubule**.
 
• The renal corpuscle contains a **tuft of capillaries** called a **glomerulus** and is surrounded by** Bowman's capsule**.
 
• A **healthy adult **has **1 to 1.5 million nephrons in each kidney**.
 
• The **three principal functions** of nephrons are:
 
 
• **Filtration**
 
• **Reabsorption**
 
• **Secretion**.
 
 
 
 
 
• **The cerebrum** consists of the **two hemispheres divided by a central fissure**.
 
 
• The **uppermost part** of the human brain is the **cerebrum**.
 
• It is made up of **two cerebral hemispheres** and their **cerebral cortex cortices i.e the outer layers of grey matter and the underlying region of white matter**.
 
• Its **subcortical **structures comprise of the **hippocampus, basal ganglia, and olfactory bulb**.
 
 
 
• **The cerebellum** is also known as the **little brain**.
 
 
• It is situated at the** back of the brain** underlying the **occipital and temporal lobes of the cerebral cortex**.
 
• It accounts for **approximately 10% of the brain's volume and contains 50% of the total number of neurons in the brain**.
 
• If the cerebellum is damaged it can lead to:
 
 
• **Loss of coordination of motor movement is scientifically known as asynergia**.
 
• **The inability to judge distance and when to stop is scientifically known as dysmetria**.
 
• **The inability to perform rapid alternating movements which are scientifically known as adiadochokinesia**.
 
• **Movement tremors which are scientifically known as intention tremor**.
 
• **Staggering wide-based walking is scientifically known as ataxic gait**.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are true about the brain?

(i) The main thinking part of the brain is the hindbrain

(ii) Centres of hearing, smell, memory, sight, etc are located in the forebrain.

(iii) Involuntary actions like salivation, vomiting, and blood pressure are controlled by the medulla in the hindbrain

(iv) Cerebellum does not control posture and balance of the body
questions.solution:
**__CONCEPT:__**

__
 
• The brain is the central information processing organ of our body, and acts as the '**command and control system**'.
 
• It controls **voluntary movements, the balance of the body, the functioning of vital involuntary organs, and the activities of some endocrine glands and their secretions**.
 
• The brain plays a crucial role in **thermoregulation, homeostasis, hunger, thirst, circadian rhythms of the body, and also animal behaviour**.
 
• The brain is also the **site of the processing of vision, hearing, speech, memory, emotions, thoughts, and intelligence**.
 
• The human brain is protected by the skull and divided into 3 major parts - **forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain.**

**EXPLANATION:__**

**Statement (i)** - The main thinking part of the brain is the hindbrain.

 
• The main thinking part of the brain is the** cerebrum**, and it forms the major part of the human brain.
 
• The cerebrum is one of the parts of the **forebrain**.** Thalamus and hypothalamus** are also parts of the forebrain.

**Hence, this statement is incorrect.**

**Statement (ii) **- Centres of hearing, smell, memory, sight, etc are located in the forebrain.

 
• The forebrain consists of the cerebrum, thalamus, and hypothalamus.
 
• Centers of hearing, smell, memory, sight, etc are located in the** forebrain**.
 
• It also contains a number of centers that control body temperature, and the urge for eating, and drink.

**Hence, this statement is correct.**

**Statement (iii)** - Involuntary actions like salivation, vomiting, and blood pressure are controlled by the medulla in the hindbrain.

 
• The hindbrain comprises the pons, cerebellum, and medulla.
 
• Involuntary actions like salivation, vomiting, and blood pressure are controlled by the medulla oblongata.
 
• The medulla also contains centers that control respiration, cardiovascular reflexes, and gastric secretions.

**Hence, this statement is correct.**

**Statement (iv) **- Cerebellum does not control the posture and balance of the body.

 
• The cerebellum is a part of the hindbrain and is located near the brainstem.
 
• The cerebellum controls the posture and balance of the body.
 
• It is also responsible for coordinating voluntary movements of the body.

**Hence, this statement is incorrect.**

**So, the correct answer is option (3).**

questions.question: Largest gland in the human body is ____________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Liver**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The liver is the largest Exocrine gland in the body.
 
• It weighs about 1.5 kg.
 
• It is situated on the right side of the body.
 
• Many toxic waste products, as well as excretory products, are produced in the liver.
 
• It also produces proteins like Prothrombin and Fibrinogen and Vitamins like A, D, K, and B12.
 
• Heparin, Urea, and Bile Juice are produced in the liver.
 
• The liver is only present in Vertebrate animals.
 
• Iron is stored in the liver in the form of 'Ferritin' while glucose is stored in the form of "Glycogen".
 
• "Kupffer cells work as a scavenger for micro-organisms in the liver and also help in eliminating toxic substances.
 
• Waste products such as Urea, Uric Acid, Creatine, and Bilirubin are produced in the liver.
 
• Many factors such as Bile Juice, fatty acids cholesterol, phospholipids and also 50% of lymph in the body are produced by the Liver only.
 
• Most of the metabolic processes in the body such as Glycogenesis (conversion of Glucose to Glycogen), Glycogenolysis(conversion of Glycogen to Glucose), Gluconeogenesis(formation of Glucose from noncarbohydrate substance), Deamination(conversion of ammonia to Urea) are carried out in the liver, that's why liver is considered as 'Busy Organ'.
 
• The liver is supplied by both oxygenated as well as deoxygenated blood.
 
• The rate of blood supply to the liver is 1500ml/min.(1000ml deoxygenated +500ml oxygenated).
 
• The artery providing blood supply to the liver is known as the Hepatic artery.
 
• The major supply of blood to the liver is by 'portal vein'(75%) & the remaining (25%) by the Hepatic artery. That is why the liver is known to have a 'Dual blood supply.
 
• Maximum blood is stored in 'liver' in human beings while in frogs it is stored maximally in the 'Spleen'.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Structure of the Brain:** For the convenience of study, the brain can be divided into three parts: **Hindbrain, Midbrain and Forebrain**

questions.question: In human beings, certain chemicals which cross the synapse between nerve cells are released from
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**option 4**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **__Important Points__**

__
 
• The end portions of the **axon** have swollen ends like “**bulbs**” which store

 **chemicals called neurotransmitters**.
 
• **Axon** bulbs are closely placed near the dendrites of another neuron.
 
• This junction of two neurons is called a **synapse** and the **space at the synapse that separates **the two neurons is called the **synaptic cleft**.
 
• Through the **synapse**, the impulse passes from one neuron to the next neuron.
 
• When an **impulse** reaches the end of the first neuron, a **neurotransmitter** is released in the synaptic cleft of the **synapse**.
 
• These chemicals cross the gap or synapse and start a similar electrical impulse in the next neuron.
 
• Finally, the **impulse** is delivered from neurons to other cells, for example, the muscle cells or glands to elicit the desired action.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **Key Points__**

__
 
• **Chemical synapses** are specialized junctions through which cells of the nervous system signal to one another and to non-neuronal cells such as muscles or glands.
 
• Chemical synapses allow the neurons of the central nervous system to form interconnected neural circuits.
 
• A chemical synapse between a motor neuron and a muscle cell is called a neuromuscular junction.
 
• They also provide the means through which the nervous system connects to and controls the other systems of the body.
 
• They are thus crucial to the biological computations that underlie perception and thought.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** 

 
• A **stimulus** is an agent or an environmental change that can initiate a response in the body.
 
• The stimuli can be of several types. It could be physical (touch, prick, pressure), auditory, chemical, radiant (light), heat or cold, or electrical.

questions.question: Which of the following organs is not controlled by the Autonomous Nervous System?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is** Eye.**

**Explanation:-**

__
 
• **Glands:** Controlled by the autonomic nervous system. The ANS regulates the secretion of various glands, including salivary glands, sweat glands, and endocrine glands.
 
• **Heart:** Controlled by the autonomic nervous system. The ANS regulates heart rate and cardiac function through sympathetic and parasympathetic inputs.
 
• **Eye:** Not primarily controlled by the autonomic nervous system. The muscles responsible for voluntary eye movements are controlled by the somatic nervous system. However, certain autonomic reflexes, such as the pupillary light reflex and accommodation reflex, involve the ANS.
 
• **Uterus:** Controlled by the autonomic nervous system. The ANS regulates uterine contractions during labor and delivery, as well as other functions of the female reproductive system.

 

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

**Autonomous Nervous System**

__
 
• It is a** complex set of neurons** that mediate** internal homeostasis without conscious intervention or voluntary control.**
 
• The** ANS maintains blood pressure**, regulates the rate of breathing, influences digestion, and urination, and modulates sexual arousal.
 
• There are two main branches of the **ANS** – the sympathetic nervous system and the parasympathetic nervous system.
 
• The Autonomic nervous system is of two types **sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system**
 
• The **sympathetic nervous system** is associated with flight or flight responses this is characterised by the release of large quantities of epinephrine from the adrenal gland an increase in heart rate an increase in cardiac output skeletal muscle dilation cutaneous and gastrointestinal contraction pupillary dilation bronchial dilation piloerection occurs.
 
• The** Parasympathetic nervous system** predominates in quiet rest and digestion conditions the main purpose of the parasympathetic nervous system is to conserve energy to be used later and regulate bodily activities like digestion and urination.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/47afd9f5ca5e5b4954f81e31043840c8e9a82195c161752c5548c0191134cea7.png] 

The nervous system in humans

 
• Central Nervous System
 
• Peripheral Nervous System

Central nervous system:-

 
• The part of the nervous system that controls the whole body and the nervous system itself is called the central nervous system.
 
• The central nervous system is made up of the brain and spinal cord.
 
• The sensations received from the nerves in these organs are analyzed.

Peripheral nervous system-

 
• The peripheral nervous system is the part of the nervous system made up of sensory neurons and other neurons that connect the central nervous system to the peripheral nervous system.
 
• It has only a group of nerves, which extends from the spinal cord to the organs on both sides of the body.
 
• The peripheral nervous system includes all the nerves that originate from the brain and spinal cord.
 
• The peripheral nervous system is divided into two parts-

 
• Somatic Nervous System
 
• Autonomous Nervous System

questions.question: In reflex action, reflex arch is formed by
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Receptor → Spinal cord → Muscle.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• In the reflex action, the reflex arch is formed by Receptor → Spinal cord → Muscle.
 
• The correct circuit of the reflex arc is Receptor→sensory neuron→spinal cord→motor neuron→effector
 
• A **reflex arc is a neural pathway that controls a reflex action. In vertebrates, instead of passing directly to the brain, the sensory neuron's synapse in the spinal cord.
 
• This helps in a faster reflex action** without the delay that is caused by routing signals through the brain.
 
• The three main types of neurons are sensory, motor and relay neurons.

 [IMAGE: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/Imgnotra%C3%A7at_arc_reflex_eng.svg/280px-Imgnotra%C3%A7at_arc_reflex_eng.svg.png] 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

The **detailed process is**

 
• The receptor detects a stimulus.
 
• Sensory neurons send electrical impulses to a relay neuron located in the spinal cord.
 
• Relay neurons connect sensory neurons to motor neurons.
 
• Motor neurons send an electrical impulse to an effector.
 
• Effector produces a response.
